goal: Get comfortable with Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes so I can port a small Go CLI tool
interpretation: After about 4 hours of watching, the learner can reason about Rust ownership, borrowing and lifetimes with confidence, use Result and the ? operator idiomatically, and port their small Go CLI tool to Rust.
assumptions: The learner needs enough Rust syntax and tooling (cargo, structs, enums, match) to follow videos, but this is covered by mapping from Go rather than taught from scratch.
Traits are needed mainly as they relate to error handling, generics bounds and lifetimes, not as a full deep dive.
The ported CLI uses typical pieces: argument parsing (e.g. clap), file or stdin IO, and error propagation.
Videos in English; the learner prefers material aimed at experienced developers coming from Go, C, or C++.

sub_topics.title: Rust orientation for Go developers (cargo, structs, enums, match, Option)
sub_topics.why: Gives the minimum Rust vocabulary and tooling to follow ownership examples, mapped onto Go concepts they already know, without re-teaching variables or loops.

sub_topics.title: Ownership and moves (stack vs heap, move semantics, Copy vs Clone, Drop)
sub_topics.why: Go's GC hides ownership; this learner knows pointers and memory so can grasp move semantics quickly, but must internalize who owns and frees data.

sub_topics.title: Borrowing and references in depth (shared vs mutable borrows, borrow checker rules, common errors)
sub_topics.why: They want depth on the borrow checker; they need to understand aliasing XOR mutability and how to fix typical compiler errors, contrasted with Go pointers and slices.

sub_topics.title: Lifetimes (annotations, elision rules, structs holding references, 'static)
sub_topics.why: Lifetimes are the hardest part for newcomers and are needed for structs and functions that return references, such as parsed CLI config.

sub_topics.title: Traits and generics essentials (impl Trait, trait bounds, From, Display, Error trait)
sub_topics.why: Idiomatic error handling relies on traits such as std::error::Error, From and Display, which are unlike Go interfaces in key ways.

sub_topics.title: Error handling with Result and the ? operator (custom error types, thiserror, anyhow, From conversion)
sub_topics.why: Their Go CLI returns errors everywhere, so they need to translate if err != nil patterns into Result, ?, and custom or anyhow errors.

sub_topics.title: Build a Rust CLI project (clap, file IO, error propagation, ownership in practice)
sub_topics.why: A project-style walkthrough shows ownership, borrowing, lifetimes and Result working together in a tool like the one they are porting.

picks.title: Rust for Go Developers: The 6 Things You Actually Need to Learn
picks.reason: A short orientation written for Go developers. It maps ownership, borrowing, Result/Option and the ? operator onto what a Go engineer already knows, and it frames the compiler as a teaching tool. It is a light overview (flagged surface_intro), but it is the only candidate aimed at Go developers. Skip the async/Tokio and crate-ecosystem sections.

evidence.quote: Who owns this data right now? The string's ownership moved into the prepare job function.
If the function only needs to read the text, borrow it. We change the parameter to a borrowed string slice.
When a borrow fails, identify which value owns the data. When a future isn't send, inspect what state is being held.

picks.confidence_note: Right audience, but shallow. It only sets the stage for the rest. Confidence would be higher if a longer Go-to-Rust bridge video existed.

picks.title: Understanding Ownership in Rust
picks.reason: Walks through the ownership rules, move vs Copy, Drop, passing and returning ownership, then references and the one-mutable-reference rule, with compiler errors shown. It gives the mechanics of moves and Drop that the Go learner lacks. The unflagged transcript shows it staying at a working-programmer level.

evidence.quote: each value in rust has a variable that's called its owner so one variable one owner
instead of calculate length taking a string we'll make it take a reference to a string
you can only have one mutable reference to a particular piece of data in a particular scope

picks.confidence_note: Clear, complete coverage of moves and basic borrowing. The stack/heap section is partly review for this learner.

picks.title: The promise of Rust
picks.reason: Contrasts Rust's moves and borrows with Go and JavaScript semantics. It explains the aliasing-XOR-mutability rule behind the borrow checker and where the checker is too conservative, plus the Rc/RefCell and Arc/Mutex escape hatches. This gives the depth on the borrow checker the learner asked for. Skip the sponsored segment.

evidence.quote: Copy trait. i64 does implement Copy because copying an integer from one register to another is very fast.
String type specifically with a capital S refers to a valid UTF-8 sequence stored somewhere on the heap.
Rust compiler rejects an infinity of programs that are memory safe and useful, but that it simply isn't able to verify as such.

picks.confidence_note: Strong fit for a senior Go developer. It overlaps somewhat with the previous video on moves, which is deliberate reinforcement.

picks.title: The Secret Behind Rust’s Memory Safety: The Borrow Checker EXPLAINED
picks.reason: A compact drill on the borrow checker's one-mutable-or-many-immutable rule, scoped borrows, dangling references and common errors with fixes. It consolidates the rules before lifetimes and bridges into reference lifetime tracking.

evidence.quote: you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references, but not both at the same time
the borrow checker uses lifetime analysis to figure out how long references live and ensures that no reference outlives the data it points to
the borrow checker ensures you're not using data while it's mutably borrowed elsewhere

picks.confidence_note: Short and some overlap with earlier picks. It is useful as a consolidation of common errors.

picks.title: Rust Lifetimes Explained — Finally Make Sense of 'a (2026)
picks.reason: Frames lifetime annotations as describing relationships between references, not controlling memory. It covers the longest() problem, the three elision rules, struct lifetimes, 'static and higher-ranked bounds. It is the unflagged member of its near-duplicate cluster.

evidence.quote: Lifetime annotations do not change how long a value lives. They do not control memory. They do not affect runtime behavior in any way.
By marking both inputs and the output with tick a, you are telling the compiler that the returned reference will live at least as long as the shorter of the two inputs.
Static does not mean forever. It means contains no borrowed references that could become invalid.

picks.confidence_note: Covers every lifetime sub-topic in the plan. Structs holding references get only a brief treatment.

picks.title: Rust Powered Polymorphism ⚡️ With Traits
picks.reason: Explains traits as Rust's analogue of interfaces, covering default implementations, static dispatch with generics vs dynamic dispatch with dyn, and supertraits. This maps directly onto Go interfaces and gives the trait background needed for error types. Flagged surface_intro, but it is short and no unflagged candidate covers dyn vs generics.

evidence.quote: instead of interfaces Rust has something called traits which are very similar to interfaces but with some subtle differences
dyn refers to something called Dynamic dispatch which is in contrast to something called Static dispatch

picks.confidence_note: Good Go-interface mapping, but light on trait bounds and From/Display, which the next picks cover.

picks.title: Introduction to Generics and Traits | Advanced Rust Part 1
picks.reason: Covers generic functions, trait bounds, why the compiler demands bounds like Copy/Add, and how to implement traits manually. This supplies the bounds mechanics that Display/From/Error-based error handling relies on. Flagged pure_theory, but that does not conflict with this learner's constraints.

evidence.quote: traits or interfaces as they are called in most other languages are Concepts that guarantee that an object or struct provides a certain functionality
we need to make sure that the copy trait is implemented and we do this by adding the copy trait as a requirement for our type T

picks.confidence_note: The generic sum example is basic for a Go developer who already knows generics, but the bounds material is needed. Remaining trait topics (From, Display, Error) come from the Result videos.

picks.title: A Simpler Way to See Results
picks.reason: Builds Result from sum types, then covers the ? operator, collecting Results, designing custom error types and combining errors with From. It also shows thiserror and anyhow. This is the closest match to Go's if err != nil pattern and gives the conceptual model of idiomatic Result use.

evidence.quote: the question mark is a unary post-fix operator so you use it like this
if all the results are okay you get back an OK VEC but if any of them fails the whole thing fails
I would personally use the this error crate to derive a bunch of nice trait implementations all at once

picks.confidence_note: Covers custom error types and From conversion with depth. thiserror/anyhow are covered more briefly here, so the next video fills that in.

picks.title: Rust Error Handling Explained: thiserror vs anyhow (Best Practices)
picks.reason: Compares thiserror (typed enum errors for libraries) with anyhow (context-based errors for applications), with examples and a rule of thumb for choosing. This tells the learner which to use in the ported CLI.

evidence.quote: use this error when you are building libraries and crates and use anyhow when you are building applications
if it's very straightforward into the face just use anyhow if you require more complex handling then I would prefer this error

picks.confidence_note: Practical and unflagged. The segment map has timestamp irregularities, so it is slightly less certain which sections are covered.

picks.title: Build a Rust CLI Tool from Scratch (clap, serde, anyhow) – logscan
picks.reason: Builds a log-analysis CLI with clap and anyhow, and uses zero-copy parsing with &str lifetimes. It confronts a real borrow-checker error (E0515) and fixes it by moving ownership up to the caller. This is ownership and lifetimes applied in the CLI shape the learner is porting.

evidence.quote: Time and message are string slices ampersand STR that borrow directly from the file's text instead of copying it. That's zero copy parsing and it's very fast.
The idiomatic fix, move ownership up. Let the caller own the text and only borrow from it. The string lives in main, which outlives everything else.
Data must live at least as long as anything that borrows it. When the borrow checker complains, ask yourself, who owns this, and does it live long enough?

picks.confidence_note: Excellent fit. The only concern is that it is short, so it only sketches the project structure.

picks.title: 🚀 Build a Robust CLI App in Rust with Clap | Rust Programming Tutorial
picks.reason: The chosen range shows the config-handling commands taking references to an AppConfig (ownership in practice), then Result and anyhow error propagation with ? in a clap CLI. This is the longer, more realistic project code after the compact logscan example. The setup and async/Tokio parts are skipped.

evidence.quote: anyhow so this would um allow me to handle errors much more easily and elegantly
it's going to just take one thing more or less so it will take this config which should be of type so be a reference to app config

picks.confidence_note: Only part of a 70-minute tutorial is used. The range is based on the segment map, and the exact fit would need checking against the video.
